abstract: ABSTRACT Missing an entire chromosome or chromosome arm in normal diploid cells has a deleterious impact on cell viability, which may contribute to the development of specific birth defects. Nevertheless, the effects of chromosome loss in human cells have remained unexplored due to the lack of suitable model systems. Here, we developed an efficient, selection‐free approach to generate partial monosomy in human induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs). The introduction of Cas9 proteins and a pair of gRNAs induces over megabase‐sized interstitial chromosomal deletions. Using human chromosome 21 (HSA21) as a model, partial monosomy 21q (PM21q) iPSC lines with deletions ranging from 4.5 to 27.9 Mb were isolated. A 33.6 Mb deletion, encompassing all protein‐coding genes on 21q, was also achieved, establishing the first 21q monosomy human iPSC line. Transcriptome and proteome analyses revealed that the abundances of mRNA and protein encoded by the majority of genes in the monosomic regions are half of the diploid expression level, indicating an absence of dosage compensation. The ability to generate customized partial monosomy cell lines on an isogenic, karyotypically normal background should facilitate the gain of novel insights into the impact of chromosome loss on cellular fitness.
methods:
4
Experimental Procedures
4.1
Cell Culture
A subclone (HPRT
−
) derived from the human iPSC line 201B7, which was previously reported to exhibit a stable, normal diploid karyotype (46,XX), was used as the parental cell line in this study (Takahashi et al.
2007
; Uno et al.
2022
). All iPSCs were cultured on dishes coated with 0.5 μg/cm
2
iMatrix‐511 silk (Nippi, Tokyo, Japan), using StemFit AK02N (Ajinomoto, Tokyo, Japan) as medium and maintained at 37°C under 5% CO
2
. Y‐27632 (10 μM; Fujifilm‐Wako, Osaka, Japan) was also added to the medium during passages and cell thawing. The following day, the medium was changed, and Y‐27632 was removed.
4.2
RNP
Complexes and Transfection
Custom crRNAs were designed using the gRNA design tool CRISPOR (
http://crispor.tefor.net/
). Custom crRNA, tracrRNA, recombinant Cas9 protein, and electroporation enhancer were obtained from Integrated DNA Technologies (IDT; Coralville, IA, USA). The sequence information for crRNAs+PAM used in this study and their position on HSA21 (hg38) are shown in Figure
S1
. It should be noted that gRNA#1 is located at the sub‐centromeric region, the highly similar sequences of other chromosomes (HSA2, 13, and 18) may be amplified by the primer pair (Figure
S1
) used in this study. However, the PAM sequence (AGG) for gRNA#1 (GACAGGTAAGGATTACTAGGAGG) is only present in HSA21 and the corresponding sequences in other chromosomes are AGC which may not function as a PAM sequence. Therefore, this feature of gRNA#1 enables the specific cleavage of the target sequence on HSA21. Custom crRNA and tracrRNA were combined into gRNA, in accordance with the manufacturer's protocol. RNP complexes were produced at a 600:520 pmol (gRNA:Cas9 protein), in accordance with the manufacturer's protocol. Electroporation was performed on 2 × 10
6
cells at 150 V for 5.0 ms using NEPA21 Super Electroporator (NEPA Gene, Chiba, Japan).
4.3
Single‐Cell Cloning and Pool Screening
The parental iPSCs were transfected with RNP complex comprising Cas9 protein and a gRNA pair for each deletion (Figure
1a,b
). The transfected cells were seeded into six‐well tissue culture plates and cultured under nonselective conditions. One week after transfection, genomic DNA was extracted from the cells using the Gentra Puregene Cell Kit (Qiagen, Limburg, Netherlands), in accordance with the manufacturer's instructions. This DNA sample was then employed as a template for PCR analysis to detect the junction‐specific sequence generated by the deletion between each gRNA pair. The primers used for the detection of each junction‐specific sequence were as follows: 2F × 26R for ΔA, 24F × 41R for ΔB, 39F × 58R for ΔC, 58F × T9R for ΔE, 4F × 58R for ΔH, and 1F × T9R for Δ21q. The nucleotide sequence for each primer is shown in Figures S1 and S2. Once the deletion had been confirmed by PCR in samples of 1 ng of genomic DNA, the cells were subjected to single‐cell isolation in 96‐well plates by FACS (BD FACS Melody Cell Sorter; Becton Dickinson, Franklin Lakes, NJ, USA) sorting or limiting dilution. Once the cells in each well had been sufficiently propagated, the genomic DNA sample from each well was subjected to junction‐specific sequence PCR and polymorphic marker analysis to identify clones carrying the expected deletion of HSA21. The polymorphic markers were selected based on the information from the UCSC Genome Browser (
https://genome.ucsc.edu/
) and the nucleotide sequences of each primer are shown in Figure
S4
. As for the additional experiments conducted to isolate the Δ21q line, 10 cells were seeded per well of a 96‐well plate. Once the cells had reached approximately 90% confluence, they were detached with PBS/1 mM EDTA. Of the sampled cells, 90% underwent PCR analysis, while the remaining 10% were cultured further in fresh medium. The sampled cells were suspended in 80 μg/mL proteinase K and reacted at 55°C for 3–24 h. The wells positive for junction‐specific sequence PCR were identified using the crude sample after treatment. The cells from positive wells were subjected to single‐cell isolation in 96‐well plates by FACS sorting or limiting dilution.
4.4
Sanger Sequence Analysis
PCR amplification products obtained by junction‐specific PCR were purified using the gel extraction kit NucleoSpin Gel and PCR Clean‐up (MACHEREY‐NAGEL, Nordrhein‐Westfalen, Germany). The analysis was outsourced to Eurofins DNA Sequencing.
4.5
Karyotyping by G‐Banding
Cells were seeded on iMatrix‐511 silk‐coated dishes and maintained in StemFit AK02N medium until the exponential growth phase. Metaphase Arresting Solution (Genial Genetic Solutions, Chester, UK) was added 60–120 min before the end of the incubation to a final concentration of 0.25–1.0 μg/mL. The collected cells were subjected to hypotonic treatment with 0.075 M KCl for 15 min and fixed with Carnoy's fixative (methanol:acetic acid ratio 3:1). The suspended cells were dropped onto slides and dried at 65°C overnight. The slides were then treated with 0.05% trypsin for 10–45 s at 3°C–6°C, 20% FBS for 5 min, and 2% Giemsa for 7–9 min. The metaphase images were captured with Metafer software (MetaSytems, Altlußheim, Germany) using CoolCube1 CCD (MetaSytems) mounted on an AxioImagerZ2 microscope (Carl Zeiss Microscopy, Oberkochen, Germany). The G‐banded metaphases were analyzed in 20 cells per sample using Ikaros Karyotyping software (MetaSystems).
4.6
Whole‐Genome
CGH
Microarray Analysis
Each amplified sample (500 ng) was labeled with SureTag Complete DNA Labeling Kit (Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, CA, USA). In brief, Cy3‐ and Cy5‐labeled DNA was combined with Cot‐1 DNA (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA) and CGH blocking agent (Agilent Technologies), and then denatured and hybridized to the arrays (SurePrint G3 Human CGH Microarray 4× 180K; Agilent Technologies) for 24 h in a rotating oven at 67°C and 20 rpm (Agilent Technologies). After hybridization and washing, the microarray was scanned using Agilent SureScan Microarray Scanner System (G2600D). Images were analyzed with Feature Extraction Software 12.1.1.1 (Agilent Technologies), using the CGH_1201_Sep17 protocol for background subtraction and normalization. Statistical analysis of the microarray experiments was conducted using the Aberration Detection method‐2 statistical algorithm (Agilent Technologies) based on the combined log2 ratios at a threshold of 6.0, as in our previous study (Nakayama et al.
2010
). The data calls with average log2 ratios of < 0.25 were filtered to exclude false positives. Array CGH data are deposited at the Genomic Expression Archive (Kodama et al.
2019
) under accession number A‐GEOD‐10150.
4.7
Cell Proliferation Assay
For the proliferation assay, cells were seeded in triplicate into wells of 96‐well plates (2.0 × 10
3
cells/well). A total of seven plates were prepared, one for each day. The proliferation of cells was measured at 24‐h intervals for 7 days under standard feeder‐free conditions using the Cell Titer‐Glo assay (Promega, Madison, WI, USA). The data obtained from the cell count for the 96‐h period of the logarithmic proliferation phase were used to calculate the doubling times using the least‐squares method.
4.8
Transcriptome Analysis
Total RNA was isolated using NucleoSpin RNA Plus (MACHEREY‐NAGEL) 4 days after seeding in six‐well plates at 2 × 10
6
cells. Isolated RNA was treated with reverse transcriptase (TaKaRa, Kusatsu, Japan) to produce cDNA, which was analyzed using the next‐generation sequencer NovaSeq 6000 (Illumina, Sun Diego, CA, USA). Reads were mapped to the hg38 genome by Hisat2 (Kim, Langmead, and Salzberg
2015
). Gene expression was quantified using featureCounts with the hg38 refseq table as a reference. Expression was normalized using the TPM method (Harrow et al.
2012
). Data were visualized using the hg38 human genome database with the Integrative Genomics Viewer (
http://software.broadinstitute.org/software/igv/
). RNA‐seq data are deposited at the DDBJ Sequence Read Archive (Kodama, Shumway, and Leinonen
2012
) under accession number DRA019210.
4.9
Sample Preparation for Proteome Analysis
The samples were prepared as described previously (Kawashima et al.
2022
). In brief, the cells were dissolved in 100 mM Tris (pH 8.0) containing 4% SDS, 20 mM NaCl, and 10% ACN using BIORUPTOR BR‐II (SONIC BIO Co., Kanagawa, Japan). Twenty micrograms of extracted proteins were quantified using Pierce BCA Protein Assay Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific) at 200 ng/μL. Protein purification and digestion were performed using a sample preparation (SP3) method (Kawashima et al.
2022
; Hughes et al.
2019
). Tryptic digestion was performed using 500 ng/μL Trypsin Platinum (Promega) for 14 h at 37°C. The protein extracts were reduced with 10 mM TCEP and 40 mM 2‐chloroacetamide for 15 min at 80°C. The digests were purified using GL‐Tip SDB (GL Sciences, Tokyo, Japan), in accordance with the manufacturer's protocol. The peptides were dissolved again in 0.02% DMNG containing 0.1% TFA and quantified using Pierce Quantitative Peptide Assays & Standards (Thermo Fisher Scientific) at 200 ng/μL.
4.10
LC–MS/MS
The digested peptides were loaded directly using a 75 μm × 300 mm nanoLC nano‐capillary column (CoAnn Technologies, Richland, WA, USA) at 50°C and then separated with a 100‐min gradient (mobile phase A = 0.1% FA in water, B = 0.1% FA in 80% ACN) consisting of 0 min 7% B, 88 min 37% B, 94 min 70%, and 100 min 70% at a flow rate of 150 nL/min using an UltiMate 3000 RSLCnano LC system (Thermo Fisher Scientific). The eluted peptides were detected using an Orbitrap Exploris 480 MS (Thermo Fisher Scientific). The MS1 scan range was set as full scan with m/z 495–745 at a resolution of 60,000 to set Auto Gain Control (AGC) targets for MS1 as 3 × 10
6
and maximum injection time as “auto.” MS2 was collected at m/z 200–1800 and resolution of 45,000 to set an AGC target of 3 × 10
6
, maximum injection time of “auto,” and fixed normalized collision energy of 26%. The isolation width for MS2 was set to 4.0 Th, and for the 500–740 m/z window pattern, an optimized window arrangement was used in Scaffold DIA (Proteome Software Inc. Portland, OR, USA).
4.11
Data Processing for Proteome Analysis
The raw data were searched against an in silico predicted spectral library using DIA‐NN (Demichev et al.
2020
) (version: 1.8.1,
https://github.com/vdemichev/DiaNN
). First, an in silico‐predicted spectral library was generated from the human UniProtKB/Swiss‐Prot database (Proteome ID UP000005640, 20,598 entries) using DIA‐NN. The DIA‐NN search parameters were as follows: digestion enzyme, trypsin; missed cleavages, 1; peptide length range, 7–45; precursor charge range, 2–4; precursor mass range, 500–740; fragment ion m/z range, 200–1800; mass accuracy, 10 ppm; cysteine carbamidomethylation; enabled “Heuristic protein interferences,” “Use isotopologues,” “MBR,” and “No shared spectra.” Additional commands were set as follows: “mass‐acc‐cal 10” and “matrix‐spec‐q.” The protein identification threshold was set at < 1% for both precursor and protein false discovery rates (FDRs). Proteome data are deposited at the JPOST repository (Okuda et al.
2017
) under accession number JPST003356.
body:
1
Introduction
Human diploid cells maintain two sets of chromosomes, which is essential for their propagation. In general, the loss of one of the two chromosomes or chromosome arms is detrimental to cell viability and is not tolerated in normal diploid cells (Chunduri, Barthel, and Storchova
2022
; Magnuson et al.
1985
; Shahbazi et al.
2020
). Although the analysis of aneuploid preimplantation embryos showed the similar occurrence of monosomy and trisomy on any chromosome (Biancotti et al.
2012
), human embryonic stem cell (hESC) lines could not be generated from monosomic embryos, except for chromosome X (Biancotti et al.
2012
). Consistent with this, autosomal monosomies are incompatible with life and rare viable partial monosomies or segmental deletions are associated with severe clinical features (Roberson et al.
2011
). The adverse phenotypes observed in monosomic cells are likely due to haploinsufficiency of a subset of genes sensitive to copy number as well as due to revealing of recessive, loss‐of‐function mutations (Sarel‐Gallily et al.
2022
; Chunduri et al.
2021
). Meanwhile, losses of a whole chromosome or a chromosome arm have been frequently observed in malignant tumor cells, some of which have been associated with poor prognosis and resistance to treatment, suggesting that these monosomies confer a proliferative advantage (Knouse et al.
2017
; Ahn et al.
2012
).
Despite their biological and clinical importance, the consequences of chromosome losses have not been well studied. This is because substantial defects in cell proliferation and viability in monosomic cells have prevented the generation of suitable model systems to study how the loss of chromosomes or their arms influences cellular fitness (Chunduri, Barthel, and Storchova
2022
). Spontaneously occurring monosomic cells, including human embryos sampled from preimplantation genetic screening (PGS), can be used to investigate the consequences of chromosome loss (Shahbazi et al.
2020
; Biancotti et al.
2012
; McCallie et al.
2016
; Licciardi et al.
2018
). However, they lack isogenic counterparts and cannot be maintained in culture. While monosomic human cells that have lost one chromosome due to chromosome mis‐segregation during mitosis can also be used, the monosomic cells survived only when the p53 pathway was inactivated (Chunduri, Barthel, and Storchova
2022
). Given that autosomal monosomy appears to be incompatible with a functional p53 pathway, no monosomic cells have been established from diploid non‐malignant, p53‐proficient cells.
Targeted chromosome engineering with sequence‐specific endonucleases and homologous recombination has also been recognized as a promising approach to construct cells carrying large‐scale chromosomal aberrations, including chromosome loss (Ramirez‐Solis, Liu, and Bradley
1995
; Kakeda et al.
2011
). For example, the site‐directed recombinase Cre acts on the inverted loxP site on the mouse Y chromosome, resulting in loss of this chromosome and the development of XO females (Lewandoski and Martin
1997
). Targeted insertion of a TKNEO fusion gene, which encodes both thymidine kinase (ganciclovir‐sensitive) and neomycin resistance, into a single copy of a chromosome enables positive and negative selection to remove trisomy in chicken DT40 cells and human Down's syndrome‐induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) (Li et al.
2012
; Abe et al.
2021
). However, because these approaches rely on spontaneous loss of the targeted chromosome, the efficiency of isolating clones with chromosome loss is very low (estimated to be less than one clone in 10,000 cells) (Chunduri, Barthel, and Storchova
2022
). Recently, CRISPR/Cas9‐mediated chromosome cleavage has also been employed to induce the loss of an entire chromosome or chromosome arm in cancer cell lines and in human iPSCs (Essletzbichler et al.
2014
; Taylor et al.
2018
). Nevertheless, the efficiency of megabase‐scale chromosome engineering remains suboptimal even when employing CRISPR/Cas9. Furthermore, monosomic cells may exhibit diminished fitness, necessitating the use of drug resistance or growth advantage selection to isolate rare monosomic clones. Kotini et al. successfully isolated a human iPSC clone with a CRISPR/Cas9‐induced 22 Mb deletion on the long arm of human chromosome 7 (7q) by using ganciclovir selection (Kotini and Papapetrou
2020
). Eleveld et al. have also induced 65 Mb deletion on the long arm of human chromosome 11 (11q) and 53 Mb deletion on the long arm of human chromosome 6 (6q) using CRISPR/Cas9 in neuroblastoma cell lines in a highly efficient manner, showing that these deletions may confer an oncogenic advantage (Eleveld et al.
2021
). Meanwhile, given that CRISPR/Cas9 has been demonstrated to potentially induce unintended chromosomal rearrangements and overall changes in ploidy (Cullot et al.
2019
; Rayner et al.
2019
), cell lines with monosomy or partial monosomy generated by these approaches may be associated with abnormalities in chromosome(s) other than the targeted one, making it challenging to establish a causal relationship between targeted deletion and phenotypic changes. There is thus a strong need to develop a more efficient, precise, and selection‐free method to remove an entire chromosome or chromosome arm in non‐transformed diploid cells.
In the present study, we have developed an efficient, selection‐free approach to generate a partial monosomy human iPSC panel through single‐step CRISPR/Cas9‐mediated megabase‐scaled interstitial chromosomal deletions. Using chromosome 21 (HSA21) as a model, four gRNA pairs were designed to delete contiguous segments (4.5 to 11.7 Mb) encompassing most of the long arm (21q) of HSA21. The partial monosomy 21q (PM21q) iPSC lines carrying the intended deletions were isolated with high efficiency using standard single‐cell sorting by fluorescence‐activated cell sorting (FACS) after transfection of the Cas9/gRNA‐ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complex. In each PM21q iPSC line, the doubling time was comparable to that of the parental cells, the karyotype was quite stable, and chromosomes other than HSA21 appeared normal. Unexpectedly, the deletion of most of 21q encompassing all protein‐coding genes on 21q was also achieved, establishing for the first time a 21q monosomy human iPSC line. Transcriptome and proteome analyses of PM21q iPSC lines revealed that the abundances of mRNA and protein encoded by genes on the monosomic regions were predominantly half of the diploid expression level, indicating a lack of dosage compensation at the transcriptome and proteome levels. This approach is straightforward and effective for generating an isogenic human cell panel with partial monosomy in a normal karyotype background and should be widely applicable for gaining novel insights into the consequences of chromosome loss.
2
Results
2.1
CRISPR
/Cas9‐Mediated Interstitial Megabase Deletions of
HSA21
in
iPSCs
The procedure for the construction of the PM21q iPSC panel through CRISPR/Cas9‐mediated megabase deletion is outlined in Figure
1a
. Nine gRNAs were designed in the 21q genomic region (approximately 34 Mb) containing 211 protein‐coding gene sequences based on information from the UCSC Genome Browser (
https://genome.ucsc.edu/
) and the CRISPOR website (
http://crispor.tefor.net/
) (Figures
1b
and
S1
). To circumvent the expression of truncated protein fragments, gRNA sequences located within the intergenic regions were selected. The subclone (HPRT
−
) derived from the human iPSC line 201B7 (Takahashi et al.
2007
; Uno et al.
2022
), which was previously reported to exhibit a stable, normal diploid karyotype (46,XX), was used as the parental cell line in this study. We initially used four gRNA pairs (2–26: ΔA, 24–41: ΔB, 39–58: ΔC, and 58‐T9: ΔE; Figures
1b
and
S1
), each of which was predicted to result in a deletion of approximately 11.6, 8.5, 10.5, and 4.5 Mb, respectively. An RNP complex comprising Cas9 protein with each gRNA pair was introduced into parental iPSCs via electroporation (Figure
1a
). One week after transfection, genomic DNA was extracted from the cells cultured under nonselective conditions and employed as a template for polymerase chain reaction (PCR) analysis to detect the junction‐specific sequence generated by the deletion between each gRNA pair (Figures
1a
and
S2
). As a result, all four gRNA pairs yielded detectable junction‐specific PCR products in 1 ng of genomic DNA template (Figure
S2
). Given that human diploid cells contain 6.16 pg. of genomic DNA and that 1 ng of genomic DNA is equivalent to approximately 162 cells, these results indicate that there is more than one junction‐positive cell in every 162 electroporated cells. We then attempted to isolate a single cell by FACS in 96‐well plates (Figure
1a
). PCR analysis of isolated cell‐derived genomic DNA templates yielded junction‐positive clones with high efficiency, ranging from 2.4% to 18.6% for all four gRNA pairs (Table
1
). The nucleotide sequences of the junction‐specific PCR products were found to be consistent with the expected sequences generated by over megabase‐sized chromosomal deletions between the gRNA target sites, although some of them contained small additional deletions (Figure
S3
). Subsequent PCR analysis using 21q polymorphic markers in ΔA, ΔB, and ΔC clones revealed loss of heterozygosity (LOH) in most of the junction‐positive clones, with an equal loss of each allele detected (Table
1
, Figure
S4
). The G‐banding of clones ΔA (#2–3, #4–1), ΔB (#1, #2), and ΔC (#17, #29) with LOH revealed that one of the two HSA21s was apparently shortened, while all other chromosomes appeared to be normal (Figure
2a
). Although the G‐banding did not provide definitive results regarding the 4.5 Mb deletion in ΔE clones, BAC‐FISH analysis of ΔE clones (#1, #2) indicated the loss of the expected chromosomal region (Figure
S5
). In the parental cell line, it was observed that one of the two short (p) arms of HSA21 was associated with a large satellite segment (ps+) that could be identified through G‐banding or DAPI staining (Figures
2a
and
S5
). This allowed the parental origin of the deleted HSA21 to be distinguished. For instance, the ΔB clone that produces a shorter PCR product (ΔB#2) for the D21S213 polymorphic marker has a deletion in ps + HSA21, whereas the clone (ΔB#1) that produces a longer product has a deletion in HSA21 with a small satellite segment on 21p (Figures
2a
and
S4
). In subsequent experiments, one pair of PM21q iPSC clones, each of which carries the shortened ps + HSA21 and shortened HSA21 with a small satellite segment, respectively, was selected for analysis (Figure
2a
). Given that each gRNA pair can cleave at a total of four sites in two HSA21s in diploid cells, it is possible that some deletions or inversions may occur even in the apparently normal‐sized HSA21. PCR experiments to amplify genomic fragments containing gRNA sequences in PM21q iPSC clones showed no evidence of large‐scale chromosomal rearrangements in normal‐sized HSA21, although indels were observed in the majority of PM21q iPSC clones (Figures S1 and S6). To further investigate copy number variations across the entirety of HSA21 and other chromosomes, PM21q iPSC clones were subjected to comparative genomic hybridization (CGH) analysis (Agilent Human CGH Microarray Kit 4 × 180 K; overall median probe spacing 13.1 kb). The results revealed no obvious copy number variations in any of the PM21q iPSC clones tested, except for the deleted HSA21 region (Figures
2b
and
S7
).
FIGURE 1
CRISPR/Cas9‐mediated interstitial megabase deletions of HSA21 in human iPSCs. (a) Schematic illustration of the engineering of a partial 21q monosomy iPS cell panel by CRISPR/Cas9‐mediated interstitial megabase deletion. (Top) A pair of gRNA sequences are designed at both ends of the genomic region to be deleted. The locations of the gRNA pair that are designed to delete the entire 21q region (~34 Mb) are illustrated. (Bottom) The RNP complex, comprising the Cas9 protein and the gRNA pair, is transduced into normal human iPSCs via electroporation. The treated human iPSCs are cultured in standard feeder‐free conditions without any selection process. The clones are isolated by FACS and subsequently subjected to PCR analysis using a primer pair specific for the junction sequence (F‐primer and R‐primer, top) to confirm the presence of the intended deletion. (b) The positions of the nine gRNA sequences used for the engineering of PM21q iPSC lines are illustrated in accordance with the UCSC genome browser (hg38, Figure
S1
). The length of the deletion and the number of genes present within the deleted chromosome segments in the constructed PM21q iPSC lines are also shown.

FIGURE 2

2.2
Generation of
PM21q iPSC
Lines With Deletion of the Entire 21q
The successful generation of a panel of PM21q iPSC lines with deletions of several megabases or more in size, which contiguously encompass all protein‐coding sequences on 21q, prompted us to investigate whether human iPSCs tolerate single‐copy deletion of larger segments of 21q. Two gRNA pairs were used (4–58: ΔH, 1‐T9: Δ21q; Figures
1b
and
S1
), each of which was designed to result in a deletion of approximately 27.9 or 33.6 Mb, respectively. Notably, the 33.6 Mb segment to be deleted by gRNA‐1 and ‐T9 contains all 211 protein‐coding genes on 21q. For both gRNA pairs, junction‐specific PCR products were detected in 1 ng genomic DNA templates prepared from gene‐edited cells (Figure
S2
). Single‐cell isolation by FACS and PCR analysis to amplify the junction sequence yielded 14 positive clones for ΔH with an efficiency (7.3%) comparable to that observed in experiments deleting smaller 21q segments (Table
1
). The LOH was confirmed in 13 of the 14 clones by polymorphic marker analysis (Table
1
). Clones ΔH#1 and ΔH#2, which exhibited LOH (Figure
S8
), were selected for further investigation. Meanwhile, junction sequence‐positive clones for Δ21q were obtained with lower efficiency (1 clone out of 170 wells tested, Table
1
) than those observed with other gRNA pairs. To obtain a greater number of Δ21q clones, FACS was performed at 10 cells/well to identify eight additional junction sequence‐positive wells with PCR analysis of a total of 384 wells (estimated cell number: 3840) (Table
1
). Polymorphic marker (D21S213 and D21S220) analysis revealed that three of the nine Δ21q clones (E11, D1A10, 6F29) gave a single band, indicating LOH (Figure
S8
). A single larger PCR product was detected in clones E11 and 6F29, while a single smaller product was detected in clone D1A10. These observations suggest that HSA21 of different parental origin was deleted in each clone. Sanger sequencing of the junction‐specific PCR products for clones ΔH#1, ΔH#2, E11, D1A10, and 6F29 (Figure
S3
) revealed junction sequences with insertions and deletions (indels) presumably generated by CRISPR/Cas9‐mediated non‐homologous end joining (NHEJ). PCR experiments to amplify genomic fragments containing gRNA sequences in clones ΔH#1, ΔH#2, E11, and D1A10 showed the occurrence of simple deletions in the sequence adjacent to gRNAs (Figure
S6
). In clone 6F29, the intact sequence adjacent to gRNA‐1 was detectable, yet no amplified product adjacent to the gRNA‐T9 sequence was observed (Figure
S6
). This indicates that unintended chromosomal rearrangements of HSA21 occurred in addition to the targeted interstitial deletion in clone 6F29. G‐banding of the junction‐positive/LOH ΔH (#1, #2) and Δ21q (E11, D1A10) clones revealed the presence of a mini‐chromosome and an apparently normal HSA21, indicating that substantial loss of one copy of 21q is permissible in diploid human iPSCs (Figure
3a,b
). We also found that clone E11 possesses a ps + mini‐chromosome, while D1A10 possesses a mini‐chromosome with a small satellite segment (Figure
3b
). Notably, in G‐banding of junction‐positive/LOH (6F29) and junction‐positive/non‐LOH (G41B) clones, we observed a mini‐chromosome and an HSA21‐derived enlarged chromosome with 21q of approximately double the normal size, which was presumably generated through the duplication of deleted regions (Figure
S9
). In all ΔH and Δ21q clones analyzed, no abnormalities were observed in chromosomes other than HSA21 (Figures
3a,b
and
S9
). The results of the CGH analysis were in accordance with the observations made in the G‐banding analysis. The deleted regions in ΔH and Δ21q (E11, D1A10) clones were observed to be haploid, while clones 6F29 and G41B remained diploid (Figures
3c
and
S10
). Given that a 21q monosomy human cell line has not been described and eight haploinsufficient genes have been mapped to the 21q region (Sarel‐Gallily et al.
2022
), it was somewhat unexpected that the isolation of 21q monosomy human iPSCs was possible without any selection. This suggests that the entire 21q monosomy per se may not have a significant effect on the viability of iPSCs. We then determined the doubling times for PM21q iPSC clones and parental iPSCs cultured under standard feeder‐free conditions. The doubling time of all PM21q iPSC clones was found to be comparable to that of the parental iPSCs (Figure
3d
). While the impact of deleting one of the two copies of a gene may vary depending on the context, in our experimental setting it is assumed that the 21q region does not contain any genes or regulatory sequences that profoundly affect cell proliferation in a haploinsufficient manner.

2.3
The Abundance of
mRNA
Encoded by Single‐Copy Genes Present Within Monosomic Regions Was Halved in
PM21q iPSC
Lines
Loss of one copy of an entire chromosome or chromosome segment in diploid human cells can affect both the mRNA and the protein levels of genes with a haploid status. While the level of expression would be expected to be half of the diploid expression, studies have reported that expression is not necessarily proportional to the number of gene copies (Chunduri et al.
2021
; Schukken and Sheltzer
2022
; Cheng et al.
2022
). Specifically, the mRNA and protein expression levels can be shifted toward the levels in diploid cells to compensate for the dose effect of aneuploidy (Chunduri et al.
2021
). To investigate how the dosage of genes located on the deleted chromosome segments affects mRNA and protein expression, we performed transcriptome and proteome analyses of PM21q iPSC lines. Samples from these cell lines grown under standard conditions were subjected to quantitative transcriptome and proteome analyses. RNA sequencing (RNA‐seq) data with a TPM (transcripts per million) value of 5 or higher in the parental iPSC were extracted and quantitative information was obtained for 9630 genes (Table
S1
). The transcripts of PM21q iPSC lines were normalized to the average expression levels of six parental iPSC samples (experimental replicates) and presented as log2 fold changes (log2FC) aligned according to their chromosomal locations. The averaged log2FC of 9545 non‐HSA21 genes in all PM21q iPSC lines fit a normal distribution with means ranging from −0.1 to 0.07 (Figure
S11
). The log2FC data for 85 genes on HSA21 showed a reduced level of mRNA encoded by single‐copy genes on the deleted chromosome segment in each PM21q iPSC line (Figure
4a
). On average, the transcript level of monosomic genes displayed approximately 50% reduction (log2FC = −1) in PM21q iPSC lines, with means ranging from −0.73 to −1.24 (Figures
4b
and
S11
), suggesting the absence of dosage compensation at the level of mRNA expression. In contrast, the mean log2FC for disomic genes located on HSA21 in each PM21q iPSC line ranged from −0.15 to 0.07 (Figure
S11
) as expected. Note that there are four genes (
CBR1
,
B3GALT5
,
ZBTB21
,
PKNOX1
) with log2FC values greater than −0.5 (0.71‐fold change) in both Δ21q clone E11 and Δ21q clone D1A10, suggesting that these single‐copy genes may be amenable to adjustment toward a diploid expression level through the upregulation of mRNA. In addition, the transcriptome analysis yielded consistent results in the respective pair of PM21q iPSC clones with different parental origins, as identified by the presence or absence of a large satellite segment in the short arm of HSA21 (Figure
4a
).

2.4
The Abundance of Proteins Encoded by Single‐Copy Genes Exhibited a Proportional Decrease in Conjunction With the
mRNA
Abundance
To obtain protein expression data for two Δ21q lines (E11, D1A10) and two parental iPSC samples (experimental replicates), we employed single‐shot label‐free proteomics by data‐independent acquisition mass spectrometry (DIA‐MS). A total of 9854 protein counts were collected and the log2FC value was calculated using the average counts of the parental iPSC samples as a reference (Table
S2
). The log2FC data for 74 monosomic genes located on 21q were quantified and visualized as a heat map according to chromosomal position (Figure
5a
). This indicated a reduction in protein abundance of all single‐copy genes on 21q. The log2FC of non‐HSA21 genes in Δ21qE11 and Δ21qD1A10 exhibited a normal distribution with means of 0.00 and 0.04, respectively (Figure
5b
). The protein levels of monosomic genes in the Δ21qE11 and Δ21qD1A10 lines exhibited an approximately 50% reduction (log2FC = −1) compared to the level in the parental iPSC samples with means of −1.14 and −0.97, respectively (Figure
5b
). These findings are consistent with the data from the transcriptome analysis, indicating that the protein levels of genes on 21q decrease predominantly in proportion to copy number. Thus, dosage compensation of mRNA and protein abundance does not occur for the majority of monosomic genes in Δ21q lines. We also found that there are 11 genes located on 21q that exhibit log2FC values exceeding −0.5 (0.71‐fold change) in both Δ21q iPSC lines (Figure
5c
). Of these 11 genes, 10 displayed no evidence of dosage adjustment at the mRNA level (Figure
5c
). A previous study in human trisomic fibroblasts indicated that protein subunits of macromolecular complexes are attenuated by post‐transcriptional mechanisms, and thus that the expression of the proteins encoded by trisomic genes did not increase to the expected level (1.5‐fold) (Hwang et al.
2021
). In this context, by using the CORUM database (
https://mips.helmholtz‐muenchen.de/corum/
), we investigated whether these 11 proteins are annotated as components of macromolecular complexes. The results showed that 8 of the 11 (73%) proteins were defined as subunits of macromolecular complexes by CORUM, which suggests that the impact of altered copy number of these genes may be predominantly mitigated at the post‐transcriptional level, as observed in trisomic fibroblasts (Figure
5c
).

3
Discussion
Here, we have developed an efficient, selection‐free approach to generate a partial monosomy human iPSC line by CRISPR/Cas9‐mediated megabase‐scale interstitial chromosomal deletions. Four PM21q iPSC lines, each of which carries a contiguous 21q deletion of 4.5, 8.5, 10.5, or 11.2 Mb, were readily isolated by FACS of Cas9/gRNA‐RNP‐treated cells without selection. iPSC clones with 33.6 Mb deletion of the entire long arm of HSA21 could also be isolated. To our knowledge, this is the first monosomic 21q cell line in which chromosomes other than HSA21 are stably maintained in a normal diploid state. It was somewhat surprising that all PM21q iPSC lines exhibited doubling times comparable to those of parental iPSCs, as arm level monosomy was thought to negatively affect cellular fitness. Because the p53 pathway has been shown to negatively affect the proliferation of monosomic cells and monosomy is tolerated in p53‐deficient cells (Chunduri et al.
2021
), the
TP53
gene could be mutated in our parental iPSC line. However, it is unlikely to be p53‐deficient because genomic DNA sequencing and RNA‐seq to analyze the
TP53
gene sequences in the parental iPSC line confirmed that one allele has the wild‐type sequence and the other has the common germline single‐nucleotide polymorphism (P72R) (Figure
S12
) (Barnoud, Parris, and Murphy
2019
). Of note, the analyses of
TP53
mRNA and p53 protein levels in PM21q iPSC lines revealed that there were no changes in mRNA levels, but an increase in protein levels (Figure
S13
). Further studies should be required to elucidate the behavior and roles of p53 during the establishment of PM21q iPSC lines. The same study also proposed that impaired ribosome biogenesis caused by haploinsufficiency of ribosomal protein‐coding genes (RPGs) may trigger activation of the p53 pathway in monosomic cells (Chunduri et al.
2021
). Interestingly, although RPGs are distributed throughout the human genome, only HSA7 and HSA21 do not carry them. Thus, PM21q iPSC lines have normal ribosome biogenesis, and thus active p53 may not be toxic.
There is limited information on the relationship between gene dosage and mRNA and protein expression levels in normal human cells that have lost a chromosome. Transcriptome analysis of monosomic cell lines derived from the human hTERT‐immortalized, p53‐deficient cell line showed that the median log2FC for monosomic mRNA expression ranged from −0.52 to −0.75, which is higher than the theoretical value (−1.0), indicating that dosage compensation moderately ameliorated the changes in mRNA levels (Chunduri et al.
2021
). Proteome analysis of the same cell lines showed that the median log2FC for monosomic protein expression ranged from −0.26 to −0.37, indicating more pronounced dosage compensation at the protein level (Chunduri et al.
2021
). In contrast, our results from the transcriptome and proteome analyses showed that mRNA and protein expression levels for the majority of monosomic genes on HSA21 were reduced in a manner proportional to copy number. This is consistent with a recent extensive study showing that, on average, both mRNA and protein levels were elevated by 1.5‐fold in trisomy 13, 18, and 21 human fibroblasts, indicating a lack of dosage compensation (Hwang et al.
2021
). On the other hand, several genes showed log2FC greater than −0.5 at the mRNA and/or protein level in PM21q iPSC lines (Figure
5c
). While it is possible that these genes can be regulated to adjust their expression to diploid levels, there is a need for more comprehensive investigation of individual genes to elucidate the regulatory mechanisms governing their expression.
Haploinsufficient genes other than RPGs should also be an obstacle to the establishment of monosomies. Sarel‐Gallity et al. recently performed genome‐wide loss‐of‐function screening in hESCs and identified over 600 essential haploinsufficient protein‐coding genes that negatively affect cell growth in a haploinsufficient manner (Sarel‐Gallily et al.
2022
). Despite eight of these genes mapping to 21q (Figure
S14
), a single copy of each of these genes was sufficient to support the normal growth of iPSCs in our experimental setting. Further inspection of the eight genes revealed that
COL18A1
and
MCM3PA
, which are also listed as components of macromolecular complexes (Figure
5c
), exhibited proteome log2FC values exceeding −0.5 in both Δ21q iPSC lines (Figure
S14
), suggesting the occurrence of dosage adjustment at the protein level by post‐transcriptional mechanisms. In addition, the presented approach, which permits the deletion of extensive genomic regions, has revealed that the viability of human iPSCs is not significantly affected by the removal of a single copy of any 21q sequence, including not only protein‐coding genes but also non‐coding RNAs (ncRNAs) and regulatory sequences.
The efficiency of CRISPR/Cas9‐mediated megabase‐scale chromosomal deletions under nonselective conditions remains poorly understood, largely due to the fact that the majority of previous studies were conducted under selective conditions in order to facilitate the isolation of rare clones with targeted deletions (Taylor et al.
2018
; Kotini and Papapetrou
2020
). A recent report described the induction of large deletion (65 Mb) on human chromosome 11q in SKNSH neuroblastoma cells via the use of CRISPR/Cas9 (Eleveld et al.
2021
). In that study, an RNP complex comprising a pair of gRNAs and Cas9 protein was introduced into the cells to induce interstitial deletions within the chromosomal arm, which is similar to the procedure employed in our own experiments. Despite being cultured under nonselective conditions, a high frequency (> 30%) of clones with the intended deletion was observed. Importantly, it was noted that this outcome was likely due to the growth advantage conferred by the 11p deletion in SKNSH cancer cells and that the use of established cancer cells was a crucial factor in achieving the chromosomal deletion (Eleveld et al.
2021
). Thus, it remained to be determined whether it is feasible to induce large chromosomal deletions in non‐malignant, karyotypically normal cells, which are typically less tolerant to aneuploidy. In this context, our study of deleting a megabase‐sized chromosomal segment whose loss is considered to be “neutral” in terms of the effect on cell proliferation in karyotypically normal iPSCs should provide valuable information on the relationship between the efficiency of targeted deletion and the size of the deleted segment. The efficiency of PM iPSC clone isolation ranged from 2.4% to 18.6% (Table
1
), with the exception of Δ21q clones, indicating that there was no discernible correlation between the size of the deletion (4.5 to 27.9 Mb) and its efficiency. Meanwhile, a reduction in the cloning frequency was observed for the longest deletion (33.6 Mb) in Δ21q clones (Table
1
). Moreover, Δ21q clones with duplicated 21q, which retained a diploid status, were obtained at a frequency comparable to that of Δ21q clones. These observations suggest that the 5.7 Mb region included in Δ21q but not in ΔH may contain sequences that affect the frequency of the deleted clones. Although the precise mechanism underlying this phenomenon remains elusive, studies that expand the deleted region from ΔH may facilitate the identification of sequences that contribute to the reduced frequency of clones with chromosomal deletions.
As demonstrated herein, our simple and rapid approach can be broadly applied to the generation of a customized partial monosomy cell panel on an isogenic background, as well as for modeling various partial monosomy syndromes that are challenging to study due to their rarity. The use of human iPSC as a parental cell line, which can be differentiated into various tissues, also allows investigation of the impact of specific chromosomal losses on development in vitro. Notably, partial deletion of chromosome 21q is a rare genetic condition with a variety of phenotypic manifestations, including cardiac defects, developmental delay, and intellectual disability (Roberson et al.
2011
), and the severity of the clinical phenotypes depends on which region of HSA21 is deleted. The PM21q iPSC lines established in this study are expected to serve as a valuable resource for identifying candidate loci for specific phenotypes associated with the deleted regions on 21q.
If the targeted chromosomal segments contain dosage‐sensitive genes whose loss has a strong negative effect on cell proliferation, it should be challenging to isolate clones with the intended chromosomal deletion even using our approach. Nevertheless, it may be possible to quickly ascertain if the presence of two copies of a particular chromosomal region is essential for cell viability by determining whether the junction site‐specific PCR product is detectable in bulk genomic DNA samples prepared 1 week after the treatment with Cas9‐gRNA RNP (Figure
S2
). The use of a highly specific CRISPR/Cas9 system may allow an elaborate configuration of the target region to circumvent the elimination of known haploinsufficient genes (e.g., RPGs), which may contribute to the elucidation of novel haploinsufficient genes and chromosomal regions. Furthermore, this experimental platform can be used to systematically screen the sequences essential for cell growth, thereby facilitating the minimization of the human genome, which is one of the major challenges in systems biology to comprehensively understand the systems of living cells (Kurasawa et al.
2020
).
Another potential application of the current technology is in the construction of human artificial chromosomes (HACs), which are expected to be used in regenerative medicine and gene therapy (Kazuki et al.
2021
). Although we have demonstrated the utility of HSA21‐based HACs, which have several advantages as gene delivery vectors, including stable episomal maintenance and the ability to load large gene inserts, the construction of HACs remains challenging due to a complex and time‐consuming process involving modifications using non‐human animal cells (Kazuki et al.
2021
). Combined with recent advances in other chromosome engineering techniques (Uno et al.
2023
; Miyamoto et al.
2024
), HACs constructed in clinical‐grade human iPSCs using our approach to precisely delete the desired chromosomal segment should facilitate the clinical application of HACs.
The proposed methodology is expected to accelerate the construction of model cell lines for a variety of chromosome losses in a normal diploid background. The study employing the first established 21q monosomy iPSC line revealed that the mRNA and protein expression levels of the majority of monosomic genes on 21q were approximately 50% of the levels of their counterparts in diploid cells. This indicates that there are no haploinsufficient genes on 21q with respect to the growth of human iPSCs under standard culture conditions. Nevertheless, a limited number of monosomic genes appear to show adaptation to the levels observed in diploid cells, suggesting that such dosage adjustment of specific genes may contribute to maintaining the growth capacity of PM21q iPSCs.
Furthermore, our approach would facilitate the engineering of trisomic cells, such as those associated with Down's syndrome, to elucidate the pathogenesis and contribute to the development of novel therapeutic strategies. Zuo et al. have demonstrated that the elimination of an extra HSA21 in trisomy 21 iPS cells was able to be induced by CRISPR/Cas9‐mediated cleavage at the multiple sites of HSA21 (Zuo et al.
2017
). In this context, our method allows for the precise deletion of specific chromosomal regions of HSA21, thus making it a suitable method for investigating the genotype–phenotype correlation for the region responsible for Down's syndrome.
There are some limitations of this study. First, it is difficult to exclude the possibility that Cas9‐induced off‐target mutations, which are not detectable by G‐banding or array CGH, have been introduced into the PM21q iPSC lines. A comprehensive evaluation of mutations by whole‐genome sequencing using next‐generation sequencers for each of the PM21q iPSC lines would be desirable. Second, our findings are based entirely on the data obtained by using 201B7 iPSC‐derived single subclone (HPRT‐) as the parental cell line. The robustness and reproducibility of the conclusions should be confirmed using multiple cell lines in the future.
Taking the findings together, our study should open up new avenues for addressing fundamental questions regarding the consequences of chromosome loss and the identification of potential therapeutic targets for diseases associated with aneuploidy.
4
Experimental Procedures
4.1
Cell Culture
A subclone (HPRT
−
) derived from the human iPSC line 201B7, which was previously reported to exhibit a stable, normal diploid karyotype (46,XX), was used as the parental cell line in this study (Takahashi et al.
2007
; Uno et al.
2022
). All iPSCs were cultured on dishes coated with 0.5 μg/cm
2
iMatrix‐511 silk (Nippi, Tokyo, Japan), using StemFit AK02N (Ajinomoto, Tokyo, Japan) as medium and maintained at 37°C under 5% CO
2
. Y‐27632 (10 μM; Fujifilm‐Wako, Osaka, Japan) was also added to the medium during passages and cell thawing. The following day, the medium was changed, and Y‐27632 was removed.
4.2
RNP
Complexes and Transfection
Custom crRNAs were designed using the gRNA design tool CRISPOR (
http://crispor.tefor.net/
). Custom crRNA, tracrRNA, recombinant Cas9 protein, and electroporation enhancer were obtained from Integrated DNA Technologies (IDT; Coralville, IA, USA). The sequence information for crRNAs+PAM used in this study and their position on HSA21 (hg38) are shown in Figure
S1
. It should be noted that gRNA#1 is located at the sub‐centromeric region, the highly similar sequences of other chromosomes (HSA2, 13, and 18) may be amplified by the primer pair (Figure
S1
) used in this study. However, the PAM sequence (AGG) for gRNA#1 (GACAGGTAAGGATTACTAGGAGG) is only present in HSA21 and the corresponding sequences in other chromosomes are AGC which may not function as a PAM sequence. Therefore, this feature of gRNA#1 enables the specific cleavage of the target sequence on HSA21. Custom crRNA and tracrRNA were combined into gRNA, in accordance with the manufacturer's protocol. RNP complexes were produced at a 600:520 pmol (gRNA:Cas9 protein), in accordance with the manufacturer's protocol. Electroporation was performed on 2 × 10
6
cells at 150 V for 5.0 ms using NEPA21 Super Electroporator (NEPA Gene, Chiba, Japan).
4.3
Single‐Cell Cloning and Pool Screening
The parental iPSCs were transfected with RNP complex comprising Cas9 protein and a gRNA pair for each deletion (Figure
1a,b
). The transfected cells were seeded into six‐well tissue culture plates and cultured under nonselective conditions. One week after transfection, genomic DNA was extracted from the cells using the Gentra Puregene Cell Kit (Qiagen, Limburg, Netherlands), in accordance with the manufacturer's instructions. This DNA sample was then employed as a template for PCR analysis to detect the junction‐specific sequence generated by the deletion between each gRNA pair. The primers used for the detection of each junction‐specific sequence were as follows: 2F × 26R for ΔA, 24F × 41R for ΔB, 39F × 58R for ΔC, 58F × T9R for ΔE, 4F × 58R for ΔH, and 1F × T9R for Δ21q. The nucleotide sequence for each primer is shown in Figures S1 and S2. Once the deletion had been confirmed by PCR in samples of 1 ng of genomic DNA, the cells were subjected to single‐cell isolation in 96‐well plates by FACS (BD FACS Melody Cell Sorter; Becton Dickinson, Franklin Lakes, NJ, USA) sorting or limiting dilution. Once the cells in each well had been sufficiently propagated, the genomic DNA sample from each well was subjected to junction‐specific sequence PCR and polymorphic marker analysis to identify clones carrying the expected deletion of HSA21. The polymorphic markers were selected based on the information from the UCSC Genome Browser (
https://genome.ucsc.edu/
) and the nucleotide sequences of each primer are shown in Figure
S4
. As for the additional experiments conducted to isolate the Δ21q line, 10 cells were seeded per well of a 96‐well plate. Once the cells had reached approximately 90% confluence, they were detached with PBS/1 mM EDTA. Of the sampled cells, 90% underwent PCR analysis, while the remaining 10% were cultured further in fresh medium. The sampled cells were suspended in 80 μg/mL proteinase K and reacted at 55°C for 3–24 h. The wells positive for junction‐specific sequence PCR were identified using the crude sample after treatment. The cells from positive wells were subjected to single‐cell isolation in 96‐well plates by FACS sorting or limiting dilution.
4.4
Sanger Sequence Analysis
PCR amplification products obtained by junction‐specific PCR were purified using the gel extraction kit NucleoSpin Gel and PCR Clean‐up (MACHEREY‐NAGEL, Nordrhein‐Westfalen, Germany). The analysis was outsourced to Eurofins DNA Sequencing.
4.5
Karyotyping by G‐Banding
Cells were seeded on iMatrix‐511 silk‐coated dishes and maintained in StemFit AK02N medium until the exponential growth phase. Metaphase Arresting Solution (Genial Genetic Solutions, Chester, UK) was added 60–120 min before the end of the incubation to a final concentration of 0.25–1.0 μg/mL. The collected cells were subjected to hypotonic treatment with 0.075 M KCl for 15 min and fixed with Carnoy's fixative (methanol:acetic acid ratio 3:1). The suspended cells were dropped onto slides and dried at 65°C overnight. The slides were then treated with 0.05% trypsin for 10–45 s at 3°C–6°C, 20% FBS for 5 min, and 2% Giemsa for 7–9 min. The metaphase images were captured with Metafer software (MetaSytems, Altlußheim, Germany) using CoolCube1 CCD (MetaSytems) mounted on an AxioImagerZ2 microscope (Carl Zeiss Microscopy, Oberkochen, Germany). The G‐banded metaphases were analyzed in 20 cells per sample using Ikaros Karyotyping software (MetaSystems).
4.6
Whole‐Genome
CGH
Microarray Analysis
Each amplified sample (500 ng) was labeled with SureTag Complete DNA Labeling Kit (Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, CA, USA). In brief, Cy3‐ and Cy5‐labeled DNA was combined with Cot‐1 DNA (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA) and CGH blocking agent (Agilent Technologies), and then denatured and hybridized to the arrays (SurePrint G3 Human CGH Microarray 4× 180K; Agilent Technologies) for 24 h in a rotating oven at 67°C and 20 rpm (Agilent Technologies). After hybridization and washing, the microarray was scanned using Agilent SureScan Microarray Scanner System (G2600D). Images were analyzed with Feature Extraction Software 12.1.1.1 (Agilent Technologies), using the CGH_1201_Sep17 protocol for background subtraction and normalization. Statistical analysis of the microarray experiments was conducted using the Aberration Detection method‐2 statistical algorithm (Agilent Technologies) based on the combined log2 ratios at a threshold of 6.0, as in our previous study (Nakayama et al.
2010
). The data calls with average log2 ratios of < 0.25 were filtered to exclude false positives. Array CGH data are deposited at the Genomic Expression Archive (Kodama et al.
2019
) under accession number A‐GEOD‐10150.
4.7
Cell Proliferation Assay
For the proliferation assay, cells were seeded in triplicate into wells of 96‐well plates (2.0 × 10
3
cells/well). A total of seven plates were prepared, one for each day. The proliferation of cells was measured at 24‐h intervals for 7 days under standard feeder‐free conditions using the Cell Titer‐Glo assay (Promega, Madison, WI, USA). The data obtained from the cell count for the 96‐h period of the logarithmic proliferation phase were used to calculate the doubling times using the least‐squares method.
4.8
Transcriptome Analysis
Total RNA was isolated using NucleoSpin RNA Plus (MACHEREY‐NAGEL) 4 days after seeding in six‐well plates at 2 × 10
6
cells. Isolated RNA was treated with reverse transcriptase (TaKaRa, Kusatsu, Japan) to produce cDNA, which was analyzed using the next‐generation sequencer NovaSeq 6000 (Illumina, Sun Diego, CA, USA). Reads were mapped to the hg38 genome by Hisat2 (Kim, Langmead, and Salzberg
2015
). Gene expression was quantified using featureCounts with the hg38 refseq table as a reference. Expression was normalized using the TPM method (Harrow et al.
2012
). Data were visualized using the hg38 human genome database with the Integrative Genomics Viewer (
http://software.broadinstitute.org/software/igv/
). RNA‐seq data are deposited at the DDBJ Sequence Read Archive (Kodama, Shumway, and Leinonen
2012
) under accession number DRA019210.
4.9
Sample Preparation for Proteome Analysis
The samples were prepared as described previously (Kawashima et al.
2022
). In brief, the cells were dissolved in 100 mM Tris (pH 8.0) containing 4% SDS, 20 mM NaCl, and 10% ACN using BIORUPTOR BR‐II (SONIC BIO Co., Kanagawa, Japan). Twenty micrograms of extracted proteins were quantified using Pierce BCA Protein Assay Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific) at 200 ng/μL. Protein purification and digestion were performed using a sample preparation (SP3) method (Kawashima et al.
2022
; Hughes et al.
2019
). Tryptic digestion was performed using 500 ng/μL Trypsin Platinum (Promega) for 14 h at 37°C. The protein extracts were reduced with 10 mM TCEP and 40 mM 2‐chloroacetamide for 15 min at 80°C. The digests were purified using GL‐Tip SDB (GL Sciences, Tokyo, Japan), in accordance with the manufacturer's protocol. The peptides were dissolved again in 0.02% DMNG containing 0.1% TFA and quantified using Pierce Quantitative Peptide Assays & Standards (Thermo Fisher Scientific) at 200 ng/μL.
4.10
LC–MS/MS
The digested peptides were loaded directly using a 75 μm × 300 mm nanoLC nano‐capillary column (CoAnn Technologies, Richland, WA, USA) at 50°C and then separated with a 100‐min gradient (mobile phase A = 0.1% FA in water, B = 0.1% FA in 80% ACN) consisting of 0 min 7% B, 88 min 37% B, 94 min 70%, and 100 min 70% at a flow rate of 150 nL/min using an UltiMate 3000 RSLCnano LC system (Thermo Fisher Scientific). The eluted peptides were detected using an Orbitrap Exploris 480 MS (Thermo Fisher Scientific). The MS1 scan range was set as full scan with m/z 495–745 at a resolution of 60,000 to set Auto Gain Control (AGC) targets for MS1 as 3 × 10
6
and maximum injection time as “auto.” MS2 was collected at m/z 200–1800 and resolution of 45,000 to set an AGC target of 3 × 10
6
, maximum injection time of “auto,” and fixed normalized collision energy of 26%. The isolation width for MS2 was set to 4.0 Th, and for the 500–740 m/z window pattern, an optimized window arrangement was used in Scaffold DIA (Proteome Software Inc. Portland, OR, USA).
4.11
Data Processing for Proteome Analysis
The raw data were searched against an in silico predicted spectral library using DIA‐NN (Demichev et al.
2020
) (version: 1.8.1,
https://github.com/vdemichev/DiaNN
). First, an in silico‐predicted spectral library was generated from the human UniProtKB/Swiss‐Prot database (Proteome ID UP000005640, 20,598 entries) using DIA‐NN. The DIA‐NN search parameters were as follows: digestion enzyme, trypsin; missed cleavages, 1; peptide length range, 7–45; precursor charge range, 2–4; precursor mass range, 500–740; fragment ion m/z range, 200–1800; mass accuracy, 10 ppm; cysteine carbamidomethylation; enabled “Heuristic protein interferences,” “Use isotopologues,” “MBR,” and “No shared spectra.” Additional commands were set as follows: “mass‐acc‐cal 10” and “matrix‐spec‐q.” The protein identification threshold was set at < 1% for both precursor and protein false discovery rates (FDRs). Proteome data are deposited at the JPOST repository (Okuda et al.
2017
) under accession number JPST003356.
